captions.text: Rivers can grind walls of rock into dust.
They carry millions of tonnes of soil
and sand, and hold enough energy
to power entire cities.
There are long rivers,
wide rivers and deep rivers.
But by almost any measure, one river
stands above them all: the Amazon.
Its story begins high
in the Andes Mountains,
where water from glaciers
and snowfields trickles down the slopes.
Mountain streams such
as the Urubamba River join together,
forming the headwaters that will become
the greatest river on Earth.
As it crosses South America, the Amazon
is fed by more than 1,100 tributaries,
more than any other river in the world.
Some arrive as thundering waterfalls,
like those that carry water down
from the Guiana Highlands.
The Nile is usually
considered slightly longer.
But in volume,
the Amazon leaves it far behind.
Every second, the Nile pours about 5,100
cubic metres of water into the sea.
The Amazon pours about 220,000,
around 43 times as much.
In a single day, that is enough fresh water
to supply a city for ten years.
The next biggest rivers, the Congo,
the Yangtze, the Yenisei and the Paraná,
are not even close.
In the wet season,
the Amazon's floodwaters spread
across an area about the size of Germany.
Near its mouth, the river can be up
to 40 kilometres wide.
Its waters feed the largest rainforest
on Earth, covering
around five million square kilometres.
Altogether, the Amazon holds
about 20 percent of all the river water
flowing into the world's oceans.
Every year, seasonal rains flood
the lowlands around the river, creating vast
floodplains of forest standing in water.
In these slow,
muddy channels lives one of the Amazon's
most mysterious animals:
the river dolphin, which hunts fish
and crabs in water so murky
that scientists still know little about its life.
The Amazon also carries a huge load:
around three million cubic
metres of sediment
into the ocean every day.
And where the river meets the sea,
the incoming tide pushes back.
Long waves called tidal bores,
or pororocas, roll upstream,
and surfers can ride a single wave for up
to ten kilometres.
On our restless planet,
nothing stays the same for long.
Landscapes are always being carved,
worn down and reshaped.
A human life is far too short
to watch it happen.
But the results are all around us.
In dry places, the wind becomes a sculptor.
It lifts grains of sand and hurls them
against rock like a sandblaster.
In Arches National Park in Utah, this slow
attack has carved natural stone arches,
balancing rocks and flat-topped mesas
that stand like monuments in the desert.
Sometimes the wind leaves
strange shapes behind.
Hoodoos are tall spires of rock
with a cap of harder stone on top,
protecting the softer rock beneath.
In Australia, the Devils Marbles
are giant round boulders,
sandblasted over time until they seem
to balance on top of one another.
Water can be an even stronger carver.
When fast-moving water rushes
through a crack in soft rock, it can cut
a deep, narrow channel with smooth,
curving walls: a slot canyon, glowing
with light that filters down from far above.
The greatest rock carver of all
is the Colorado River.
Over millions of years, it has cut
the Grand Canyon: 446 kilometres long,
up to 29 kilometres wide, and in places
more than 1.6 kilometres deep, exposing
rocks close to two billion years old.
Its power comes from its steep slope,
the huge amount of mud,
sand and gravel it carries,
and the relatively soft rock it flows through.
Along the coast, the ocean never rests.
Waves crash against the rocks,
armed with sand and grit
that grind the cliffs away.
Over time, the base of a cliff is undercut
until the rock above collapses into the sea.
In Australia, the Painted Cliffs were carved
this way, their layers stained orange
and red by minerals.
In the coldest places on Earth,
snow falls but rarely melts.
Layer upon layer piles up,
and the weight squeezes the fluffy snow
into dense, solid ice.
Slowly, under the pull of gravity,
this ice begins to move downhill.
These giant rivers of ice are glaciers,
and as they creep,
they scour a path through the land.
At the front of a glacier, the ice can
break away with a thunderous crack.
In Argentina, the Perito Moreno Glacier
pushes into Lago Argentino,
the country's largest lake.
Huge towers of ice crash
from its wall into the water,
sending waves across the lake.
A glacier is always melting and freezing,
changing with the time of day,
the season and the climate.
When more ice forms than melts,
the glacier grows and advances.
When more melts, it shrinks and retreats.
In Alaska, the enormous Hubbard Glacier
has been advancing
for more than a hundred years.
Cruise ships that sail up
to its face look like toys.
Most glaciers move only a few centimetres
or metres a day.
But some are surprisingly fast.
The Jakobshavn Glacier
in Greenland is one of the fastest on Earth,
flowing at up to 20 metres a day
as it pours ice into the sea.
When glaciers and ice sheets reach
the ocean, great chunks break off
and float away as icebergs.
Because ice is less dense than water,
about 90 percent of an iceberg hides
below the surface.
That hidden danger has
always threatened ships.
In 1912, an iceberg sank the Titanic,
and more than 1,500 people lost their lives.
For some animals,
though, icebergs are useful.
In the Southern Ocean,
colonies of penguins hitch rides
on floating ice, resting and travelling
until hunger sends them diving back
into the sea to catch fish.
Earth's climate has always changed, and ice
ages are a normal part of its history.
During the last ice age,
so much water was locked up in ice
that sea levels fell by around 120 metres.
Woolly mammoths grazed on cold
grasslands, hunted by sabre-toothed cats.
Today, the opposite is happening
in many places.
The ice cap on Mount Kilimanjaro
in Africa is melting so fast that scientists
warn it could disappear within decades.
Deep beneath our feet lies a hidden world.
Dark caverns and winding tunnels stretch
far into the Earth, their walls decorated
with strange stone shapes.
For the brave explorers who venture down,
the rewards are some of the
most awesome sights on the planet.
Most caves are carved from limestone,
and limestone has an extraordinary origin.
Its main ingredient, calcium carbonate,
comes from the shells
and skeletons of ancient sea creatures.
Over millions of years, they piled up
on the seafloor and were pressed,
layer by layer, into solid rock.
When rainwater soaks through the ground,
it picks up carbon dioxide
and becomes slightly acidic.
This weak acid slowly dissolves limestone,
hollowing out tunnels and chambers.
Inside the cave,
dripping water leaves its minerals behind.
From the ceiling grow
icicle-shaped stalactites.
From the floor,
stalagmites rise to meet them,
often just a fraction of a millimetre a year.
Sometimes, the ground above
a hollow simply gives way.
When weakened rock collapses
into the cavern below, a sinkhole opens,
often without warning.
In Guatemala, during a tropical storm,
a sinkhole about 30 storeys deep suddenly
swallowed a three-storey building.
Caves are among the least explored places
on Earth, which is exactly why cave
explorers, called spelunkers or potholers,
find them so thrilling.
But every expedition carries real risks:
collapsing rock, freezing water, falls,
sudden floods, and getting lost in the dark.
In Gunung Mulu National Park
on the island of Borneo,
cave experts have mapped
more than 320 kilometres of passages.
Here lies the Sarawak Chamber,
the largest known cave chamber by area:
about 700 metres long
and 100 metres high.
Nearby, Deer Cave
was discovered only in 1976.
And in Vietnam, Hang Sơn Đoòng is so vast
it has its own jungle and clouds.
It is the largest cave passage ever found.
The longest cave system
on Earth is Mammoth Cave, in Kentucky.
Explorers have now mapped
more than 686 kilometres of its passages,
and they are still finding more.
Earth's crust is a treasure chest.
Many things we use every day,
from soft talcum powder
to the graphite "lead" in a pencil,
were formed deep inside it.
Getting them out takes enormous effort,
human courage and clever technology.
Our buildings are made of it.
Marble is strong and easy to carve, and has
been used for some of the most famous
buildings in history.
Iron, mixed with other elements,
becomes steel.
Aluminium is light and strong.
Gypsum, when heated, becomes plaster
for walls and chalk for blackboards.
Our machines run on it.
Copper bends easily and carries electricity
better than almost any other metal.
Nickel goes into coins and batteries.
Mercury, the only metal
that is liquid at room temperature,
was used for centuries in thermometers.
And the phone
in your pocket depends on it too.
A mineral called coltan is used
to make mobile phones.
But much of it comes from
the Democratic Republic of the Congo,
where miners often dig by hand
in dangerous ground, risking mudslides,
toxic fumes and collapsing pits,
all in conditions of extreme poverty.
Some minerals are simply beautiful.
Fluorite glows with intense colour
under ultraviolet light.
Hematite, ground into powder, became
the red paint used in ancient rock art.
And gold can be hammered thinner
than any other metal: a single gram can
be beaten into a sheet of gold leaf
a square metre wide.
The most precious of all is diamond.
Amazingly, it is made of pure carbon,
the same element
as the soft graphite in your pencil.
Arranged differently, carbon becomes
the hardest natural mineral on Earth.
The Imperial Crown of India holds
more than 6,000 diamonds.
Other elements are far less stable.
Potassium is so reactive
that it is never found pure in nature,
and it bursts into flame
on contact with water.
Reaching Earth's buried treasure can
be extremely dangerous.
On 20 April 2010, the Deepwater Horizon
oil rig in the Gulf of Mexico exploded.
Eleven workers were killed.
The rig had been drilling
beneath about 1,500 metres of water,
a task some engineers compared
to exploring the Moon.
Around five million barrels of oil poured
into the sea, causing
the largest accidental oil spill in history.
The deep ocean is the least explored place
on our planet.
It is pitch-dark, freezing cold,
and the pressure could crush a submarine.
Yet even here, life finds a way,
from colossal squid with eyes bigger
than a human head,
to fish that make their own light.
As we dive, the ocean changes.
In the sunlit zone near the surface,
there is enough light for plants to grow.
Below about 200 metres begins the twilight
zone, where only a faint glow remains.
Past 1,000 metres is the dark zone.
Below 4,000 metres lies the abyssal zone.
And deeper than 6,000 metres,
in the ocean trenches, is the hadal zone,
one of the most extreme
and least known places on Earth.
In the darkness, it snows.
Tiny bits of dead plants and animals,
called marine snow,
drift down from the waters above.
Over thousands of years,
they settle on the seabed
and build up layers of fine mud and ooze,
some of them up to 450 metres thick.
The creatures of the deep look
like they come from another world.
The Dumbo octopus flaps ear-like fins
as it hovers above the seafloor,
thousands of metres down.
Giant ostracods, relatives of tiny shrimp,
glide through the dark water
like floating lanterns.
On the ocean floor,
cracks in the crust release volcanic heat.
These hydrothermal vents,
also called black smokers,
gush mineral-rich water as hot
as 400 degrees Celsius.
Instead of sunlight,
life here runs on chemicals.
Blind shrimp, starfish,
tube worms and fish gather
around the vents like an oasis in a desert.
The deepest point of any ocean
is the Challenger Deep,
in the Mariana Trench in the Pacific.
In 1960, two explorers,
Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh, climbed
into a submersible called the Trieste
and sank nearly 11 kilometres
to the bottom.
It was one of the most dangerous
journeys ever attempted.
For more than fifty years,
they were almost alone.
Filmmaker James Cameron made
a solo dive in 2012,
and since 2019 a new submersible has
carried more explorers down.
By 2022, 27 people had reached
the Challenger Deep.
That is still only a little more than the 12
people who have walked on the Moon,
nearly 400,000 kilometres away.
Because the deep sea
is so dangerous for humans,
scientists now explore it with robots.
Remotely operated vehicles are steered
from ships on the surface,
while autonomous vehicles navigate
the seabed on their own.
With sonar, they map underwater
mountains and valleys we have never seen
with our own eyes.
